Es gilt die Datenschutzerklärung von Matterport Inc.:\nhttps://matterport.com/de/node/44.\nVisit page ▸"}, {"url": "https://cmf.hu/news/data-science-institute-established-by-cmf-and-semmelweis-university/", "text": "News | CMF\nMenu\nMenü\nHome\nAbout us\nResearch\nPublications\nNews\nPatents\nJoin us\nSupport us\nNews\nYear\nAll\nAll\n2026\n2025\n2024\n2023\n2022\n2021\n2020\n2019\nOctober 16, 2026\nMy Older Twin – What Does My Future Self Have to Say to the Present?\nBy combining modern medicine and generative artificial intelligence, a pioneering method is being developed that provides a comprehensive picture of the body's condition by analyzing the blood's entire molecular profile. A key feature of this generative AI model is its ability to flexibly adjust biological variables—such as a digital twin's age—to simulate biological time travel, allowing researchers to predict the molecular effects of lifestyle changes or aging accurately. Using in-house, closed AI systems and mass spectrometry measurements, researchers are working to integrate this test cost-effectively into routine annual checkups. The CMF team recently published a scientific paper on this topic — an interview with Kosmas Kepesidis, Lead Data Scientist at CMF.\nFirst of all, could you explain what this research is about and how it can help us better understand healthy aging?\nIn our latest publication in Digital Medicine, we study a particular type of generative AI model called a conditional generative model, which can generate artificial data in a controlled way. In principle, what we want to generate are infrared measurements, synthetic infrared measurements that are very close, very similar to the real measurements of human blood. But we would like to do it not in a random or uncontrolled way. We want control over the creation of this artificial blood-based spectra. For this reason, we built generative AI architectures that can condition on various covariates. These include demographic characteristics like sex, age, body mass index, and other parameters. With these models, we can ask generative AI to produce artificial measurements of infrared molecular fingerprints of human blood by defining the characteristics of the individuals we want to simulate. For example, if we want to simulate females at age 55, we can just do it. We show in this manuscript that this is possible.\nThe quality of these artificial measurements is very good and closely resembles the real data. So now why is this important? I mean, at first glance, it sounds a little bit like a game, right? We're playing games here. But there's more to this than just games. In reality we run clinical studies and collect blood samples, like what we did in the H4H study, to understand human health. But in many cases, some questions cannot be answered directly with real data. And because the questions are confined to the actual constraints of the particular study. What I mean by this is the following, for example, that if we want to investigate age by analyzing real data, we show that this is not an easy job, it's actually most probably impossible currently, because the duration of the longitudinal follow-up of the measurements of each individual is about 1.5 to 2 years. This is essentially the timeframe over which individuals in the H4H study are currently followed up. But we show this using regression models. We showed that the resolution of infrared spectra in age is about six years. This means the resolution is much broader than the actual per-individual data we have. We cannot investigate aging effects using the real data. And this is exactly where the generative AI comes in, right? Using conditional generative AI, we can condition on the age. We pick individuals from the H4H study and simulate their spectra in a digital-twin fashion. And what we can do is change the age of this digital twin. We show that this is possible, and the age changes in a way that reflects the correlations that we see in the real data. At the same time, we ensure that changing the digital twin's age does not alter the individual's personal characteristics, because that would be a potential problem. But our analysis clearly shows that even when we change these individuals' ages, all other person-specific characteristics remain the same at similar levels. So that means that the individuals can get older, like inside the computer, so to speak, but remain in their own bubble.\nYou mention that we have the blood molecular fingerprint. How is it different from a standard blood test?\nIn a standard blood test in routine healthcare, you typically measure a few dozen different variables, right? For example, blood-based biomarkers related to glucose levels, inflammation, kidney function, and many others. And also lipid levels to assess some heart-related conditions and so on.\nThese variables are very specific and very targeted. They target specific molecules. Our infrared fingerprinting is a little bit different, right? So what it does is it does not give us the concentration of a particular analyte — and by analyte I mean a molecule in the blood. But what we get with infrared fingerprinting is a pattern that is generated by essentially the entire repertoire of molecules in the blood. So we get a snapshot of a pattern that is built by essentially a combination and mixture of the concentrations of many, many different molecules. We cannot easily retrieve concentrations of different analytes. But what we can do is compare this pattern with patterns of different phenotypes. For example, we know what the healthy pattern looks like, we know what the pattern of lung cancer looks like, and this is an untargeted type of biomarker that can be used not only for specific types of diseases, right? But it can be used very generally.\nIn previous studies we have seen that our infrared molecular fingerprints are not targeted. And this is because we have seen that they change depending on different phenotypes or different conditions, right? We have seen that the healthy phenotype in our fingerprints is very different from lung cancer, prostate cancer, diabetes, and other conditions like high blood pressure and so on. So it is a non-targeted tool we can use to investigate deviations from the healthy state. Then, based on the pattern of alterations, we could potentially infer the direction of the change and infer a bit about the possible origin of the alteration, which might be disease-related. This is the main difference: it is not targeted to a particular disease, nor is it a biomarker associated with a single disease. But it's more like a snapshot of the individual’s health state. Because it is not targeted, we think the best application might not be direct disease detection, but more like personalized health monitoring.\nCan we see in our blood if a new diet or exercise is actually slowing down our aging?\nThis is a very good question. I do not have the answer right now, but this is exactly the direction we would like to go in. So we have two different research lines or research directions.\nOne works using real data, where we are trying to see exactly what the effect of these factors you just mentioned — lifestyle factors and so on — is on infrared fingerprints. This is important for understanding which of these factors affect our data.\nAnd the second research line, which again depends on generative modeling, is to essentially try to condition on these lifestyle factors in the same way as we condition on age, sex, and body mass index. This would let us see how a lifestyle change — such as exercise or a medication change — could, in principle, affect the molecular fingerprint of a particular individual.\nCould this help us get completely personalized longevity plans in the future?\nYes, that is our aim. This is what we are after: using real data, synthetic data from generative AI, and other methods to better understand the best application of our molecular fingerprinting approach in healthcare, where it could provide a real benefit. One primary applications is personalized health monitoring.\nWe are building a system that monitors an individual’s health at a personalized level and identifies potential deviations from their healthy state that might be caused by unhealthy aging. It is important for us not only to detect disease development, but also any state that might keep a particular individual off their path toward healthy aging. This is the direct connection to longevity.\nAnd do you see these blood tests becoming part of our routine annual checkups soon?\nThat is our target, our main goal. And this is our hope. For this reason, we do not rely only on infrared fingerprinting. We believe additional state-of-the-art metrology methods, such as mass spectrometry proteomics and metabolomics, could also contribute to our goal of building the best possible health monitoring system with current technology. We have started expanding our activities to include additional molecular measurement approaches and combine this information with our infrared molecular fingerprinting approach to build a highly trustworthy, reliable, and personalized health monitoring system that will eventually become part of routine healthcare.\nHowever, for this to happen, we need to ensure that it is also cost-effective. When you talk about health monitoring — which is not just diagnostics — the idea is to apply such a system to routine healthcare. This means it will be used in healthy individuals before they acquire a particular disease or even show any symptoms. Therefore, we need to be careful with costs, because combining all these very expensive methods would make the system extremely costly.\nFor this reason, we are also conducting AI research focused on cost-effectiveness. We are trying to build a system that is initially based on a cheaper data modality. Additionally, we will measure and collect more expensive molecular variables only if the cheaper modality indicates a deviation from the healthy state based on its analysis of the cheaper modality —and only if the potential benefit and information gain from the additional modality outweigh the costs.\nIs AI our friend or not?\nI would say that everything depends on how it is used. Every tool humanity has created throughout history depends on how people use it. Science and technology have advanced a lot, and many of these advances have been used for both good and bad, right? We aim is to use AI for good. This is what we want to do, right? For that reason, we don't rely heavily on any OpenAI tools; we build our own. We are trying to build generative AI models ourselves and apply them to our data in a controlled, closed environment. At the same time, we want to analyze the real reliability and trustworthiness of these systems thoroughly. This is important because we are talking about medicine and healthcare—a very sensitive area. We cannot just play games. This is serious, and responsibility is our top priority.\nWhat is the main takeaway of this research for people who want to stay healthy and active as they age?\nThe most obvious question is: What do we have to do in order to stay healthy as we age, and potentially live better and longer? This is the whole idea behind longevity and what people actually want. Right now, I do not really have any better answers than what your doctor would tell you. We are not yet at the point where we can answer these questions using our approach. But we are building the tools and methods so that, in a few years, we can answer these questions with high accuracy. Right now, the best I can say is what your medical doctor would tell you: that exercise, quitting smoking, and reducing or quitting alcohol intake might be a good start. Hopefully, in the future, we will have more detailed and accurate information on this topic.\nShow allShow less\nOctober 9, 2026\nCMF Research Center civil engineering works underway\nCivil engineering and foundational works for the CMF Research Center are moving full speed ahead, with completion targeted for early 2027. Once complete, this ultra-modern building complex will house state-of-the-art laser and biological laboratories, the H4H medical center, and the National Biobank.\nOctober 2, 2026\nHong Kong Secretary Visits CMF in Szeged, Highlighting Cooperation in Personalised Preventive Healthcare\nHong Kong’s Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry, Professor Sun Dong, visited the Center for Molecular Fingerprinting (CMF) in Szeged, Hungary, where researchers are developing new approaches to identify changes in health before disease symptoms appear.\nAccompanied by Hungary’s State Secretary for Science Policy and Innovation, Dr Péter Horváth, Professor Sun toured the institute’s laser laboratory and biobank. He received a briefing from Nobel Prize-winning physicist Professor Ferenc Krausz on CMF’s research and its H4H Program. Professor Krausz discussed the program’s international expansion as part of the global protecting.health initiative, which brings together CMF, Ludwig-Maximilians University of Munich, and the University of Hong Kong. The latter represents an important step in taking the research beyond Europe.\nProfessor Sun said the Hong Kong delegation was honoured that one of the project’s key stages would take place in Hong Kong.\nThe visit offered a close look at a research programme built around a simple but potentially transformative idea. Instead of relying only on comparisons with population-wide reference values, researchers aim to follow molecular changes within the same individual over time.\nProfessor Sun praised the “state-of-the-art technology and CMF’s truly personalised approach, which could be the answer to the biggest challenges in modern medicine.”\nHong Kong as potential Asia-center of an international research network\nProfessor Sun’s visit to Szeged came during an official trip to Hungary to deepen cooperation in innovation and technology.\nAt CMF, the discussion shifted from broad scientific cooperation to a tangible example: a research program where Hong Kong could contribute directly to developing and internationally validating new approaches to personalized health monitoring.\nFor Professor Krausz, international participation is essential. Large-scale longitudinal studies require diverse populations, long-term sample collection and close cooperation between scientific and clinical institutions.\nThe expanding collaboration with Hong Kong therefore represents more than a geographical extension of the research. It provides an opportunity to test whether an approach based on tracking each person’s own molecular changes can work across different populations and healthcare environments.\nThe goal remains ambitious: to understand personal health well enough to recognise when it begins to change — and, ultimately, to see disease coming before it becomes disease.\nSeptember 21, 2026\nThree Nobel Laureates Join the Scientific Advisory Board of CMF\nThree Nobel Prize-winning researchers are joining the Scientific Advisory Board of the Center for Molecular Fingerprinting (CMF), led by Nobel Prize-winning physicist Ferenc Krausz: cell biologist Randy Schekman, pharmacologist Louis J. Ignarro, and optical physicist Donna Strickland. With their appointment, the Board will now include four Nobel Laureates. Coinciding with the announcement, Hong Kong’s Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry and Hungary’s State Secretary for Science and Innovation jointly visited CMF’s laser laboratory and biobank in Szeged.\nRegarding his appointment, Louis J. Ignarro said: \"Early detection, early intervention, and therefore prevention represent the logical path to follow. Although I am very excited about the possibility of detecting changes in health earlier, how to do this will require that we ‘think outside the box.’ There are many obstacles along the way, and we need to understand exactly what we are detecting and what it means. I’m looking forward to serving on the board, where many new ideas are likely to erupt.\"\nSteven Chu highlighted: \"It’s really the changes in a particular individual that are more significant. You don’t need to wait until the change is outside the norm of the group anymore. It gives you an earlier window. It’s a new technology, it’s a very powerful technology, and it has the potential of really changing healthcare diagnostics and prognosis. If you catch disease early, you’re in the best position to be treated.\"\nSeptember 16, 2026\nNew state-of-the-art mass spectrometry laboratory opened\nThe CMF's new laboratory was officially opened at the Centre for Advanced Laser Applications in Garching. With the installation of seven new high-resolution mass spectrometry systems from Waters Corporation, the research center now boasts a unique technical infrastructure. Nobel laureate Prof. Dr. Ferenc Krausz, along with Dr. Zoltán Takáts, a world-leading expert in metabolomics and lipidomics, and Dr. Virág Sági-Kiss, the head of the laboratory, attended the event.\nFerenc Krausz emphasized that “I’m extremely excited about this. I couldn’t actually express in words how excited I am and how happy I am and how confident I am that this is allowing us to incredibly broaden our prospects for creating the basis of future precision prevention care.”\nThe new instruments function as precise molecular scales, allowing researchers to analyze the composition of blood samples from the H4H Program. The results obtained via mass spectrometry are combined with CMF’s proprietary laser-based technology. This complex approach can detect subtle physiological changes, potentially enabling identification of chronic diseases before symptoms appear.\nZoltán Takáts highlighted that we are “on this mission to change global healthcare, to really redefine how doctors treat patients, or rather prevent diseases from developing. This is an opportunity to keep people healthy and happy throughout the decades, or maybe over a century.”\nYou can watch the video about the event by clicking on the link bellow:\nOpening the black box of human biology\nShow allShow less\nSeptember 1, 2026\nMass spectrometry systems delivered to CMF’s CALA lab\nCMF’s laboratory at the Centre for Advanced Laser Applications in Garching has received a delivery of seven Waters G3 high-resolution mass spectrometry systems, dedicated to metabolomics and lipidomics analysis. Installation and laboratory setup will take place over the coming months, before the systems become fully operational.\nOnce operational, the platform will be applied to H4H blood samples, working alongside CMF’s laser-based Infrasampler technology to provide H4H with a more complete, multimodal molecular profile for each sample.\nDr. Virág Sági-Kiss will head the new metabolomics and lipidomics laboratory.\nThe opening of the new laboratory marks an important step towards strengthening H4H’s ability to detect biomarkers associated with chronic disease.\nAugust 17, 2026\nExtending Molecular Fingerprinting into the THz Regime\nResearchers from the Laser Division at the Center for Molecular Fingerprinting (CMF) have contributed to a new study that significantly expands the spectral range accessible for molecular fingerprinting. Published in Optics Express, the work demonstrates a field-resolved spectrometer that simultaneously covers frequencies from 1 THz to the mid-infrared, opening new opportunities for investigating molecular structure and dynamics.\nUntil now, molecular fingerprinting has primarily relied on the mid-infrared spectral region. By employing organic nonlinear crystals together with compact Cr laser oscillators, the researchers generated and detected broadband THz pulses spanning from 1 to 39 THz (7.7 to 300 µm). This enables simultaneous access to the complete THz and mid-infrared molecular fingerprint region within a single measurement, providing an unprecedented spectral window for analysing molecular systems.\nThe THz spectral range offers complementary information to conventional infrared spectroscopy because it probes collective molecular motions, including backbone vibrations, large-scale structural fluctuations and intermolecular interactions in solution. These low-energy excitations provide insight into the organisation and flexibility of entire molecular assemblies that cannot be captured in the mid-infrared alone.\nThe study therefore represents an important technological advance for molecular fingerprinting. Extending spectroscopic coverage into the THz regime broadens the molecular information that can be obtained from biological samples and may contribute to future biomedical applications, including the identification of disease-related molecular signatures.\nBuilding on this work, CMF researchers are further developing time-domain THz spectroscopy for the analysis of blood plasma samples, exploring its potential to complement established molecular fingerprinting approaches in early disease detection.\nPublication: 1-THz-to-mid-infrared field-resolved spectrometer driven by a Cr oscillator\nAugust 14, 2026\nPartner initiative BIRD reports promising results on infrared molecular fingerprinting for prostate cancer detection\nCan infrared spectroscopy reveal molecular features of prostate cancer beyond those captured by prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing? Researchers from the CMF partner initiative Broadband InfraRed Diagnostics (BIRD) have addressed this question in a new study, now in press in the European Journal of Cancer.\nLed by Prof. Mihaela Žigman of the LMU Faculties of Physics,[DG1.1] in close collaboration with Prof. Christian Stief of the Department of Urology at LMU University Hospital, the researchers analysed blood plasma samples from 2,024 participants in the prospective Lasers4Life cohort. By combining infrared molecular fingerprinting (IMF) with machine learning, the team investigated whether a single blood-based measurement could identify molecular signatures associated with prostate cancer beyond the information provided by established PSA testing.\nThe results suggest that infrared molecular fingerprinting provides clinically relevant information that complements established diagnostic approaches. While IMF did not outperform PSA across the full study cohort, the findings indicate that it may provide additional molecular information in situations where PSA alone is less informative. Rather than replacing the established biomarker, IMF could therefore support clinical decision making as a complementary analytical tool.\nThe study represents another important milestone for the BIRD initiative and highlights the value of interdisciplinary collaboration between molecular science, clinical medicine and data science. It builds on the long-standing partnership between the Faculty of Physics at LMU and the Department of Urology at LMU University Hospital, as well as the dedicated work of the Lasers4Life clinical team.\nAs a close scientific partner of BIRD, CMF shares the overarching goal of advancing infrared molecular fingerprinting towards clinical applications. Studies such as this demonstrate the growing potential of molecular fingerprinting approaches to complement existing diagnostic methods and contribute to the future of precision medicine.\nOriginal publication: https://lnkd.in/dnn3-phT\nAugust 8, 2026\nMedical Deep Learning: CMF-experts at BIOMED-DATA 26\nDr Kosmas Kepesidis, our Chief Data Scientist, and Zita Zarándy, Data Scientist and PhD candidate, represented CMF at this year’s BIOMED-DATA Summer School in Budapest, where they delivered lectures and practical training sessions on the medical applications of deep learning.\nAs part of the programme, Kosmas delivered a lecture series on Deep Learning for Unstructured Medical Data. The course introduced participants to modern deep-learning methods for analyzing complex biomedical data, including medical images and clinical text.\nZita Zarándy led a series of hands-on tutorials on the same topic, guiding participants through the implementation of the presented methods and their application to practical problems.\nBy combining theoretical foundations with practical training, the course demonstrated how artificial intelligence can help extract clinically relevant information from complex medical datasets. The contribution also strengthened the exchange between CMF and the wider biomedical data science community.\nAugust 7, 2026\nLaser Science Division Researcher Presented at IMAMPC 2026\nSanchi Maithani, a researcher from our Laser Science Division gave a presentation at the 15th International Meeting on Atomic and Molecular Physics and Chemistry (IMAMPC) held at the Paul Scherrer Institute, in Villigen, Switzerland. She presented the journey of the Infrasampler laser system in Szeged to the measurement results from a pilot study of H4H samples for subject individuality analysis.\nThe conference mainly covered chemical and biological applications of ultrashort laser pulses spectrally ranging from X-rays to the infrared. It provided insights into the technical aspects of laser systems development as well as the exposure to the latest emerging applications. It also involved a tour to the labs at the Swiss Light Source (the Synchrotron facility) and Swiss FEL systems encompassing few of the most advanced ultrashort laser sources in the world.\nJuly 31, 2026\nAutomated Cryogenic Storage in Practice: CMF Biobank Reports Positive Results\nEarly this year, CMF started using Askion’s automated cryogenic storage units at its Szeged biobank to store blood plasma samples from the H4H program. Since then, the benefits have become clear. We have made sample handling more efficient, significantly reduced manual work, while cryogenic storage ensures the long-term molecular integrity of blood plasma samples.\n\"The past few months have clearly demonstrated that the automated system represents a new level in biobank sample handling,\" said Dr. Diána Debreceni, Head of the CMF Biobank Division. Sample picking, retrieval, and storing are now fully automated by robotic arms in a closed and controlled environment. As a result, manual sample selection has been virtually eliminated. This not only makes workflows faster and more efficient, but also significantly reduces the risk of human error.\nA key advantage of the system is its cryogenic storage temperature of −150°C, achieved with a liquid nitrogen–based cooling medium. This ensures long-term preservation of biological samples, allowing the structural and molecular state of blood plasma samples to remain unchanged for decades.\nOperational experience has also confirmed a significant increase in storage capacity. The Askion storage units can accommodate up to one million sample tubes, enabling the CMF Biobank to meet growing research demands well into the future.\n\"The combination of high storage capacity and full automation provides the biobank with security and flexibility that will be essential for our long-term research over. We have built an infrastructure that not only supports our current projects, but is also prepared for the scientific and diagnostic challenges of the future,\" said Dr. Diána Debreceni.\nJuly 16, 2026\nBehind every fingerprint – a protocol\nSeveral years ago, the attoworld BIRD team at LMU, a cooperation partner of CMF, began by asking a simple question. What is required take make blood-based Infrared Molecular Fingerprinting (IMF) reliable enough for robust clinical studies?\nThe honest answer turned out to be that it takes a village. Molecular biologists, physicists, biotechnologists, data analysts, and study coordinators all had a hand in figuring out how each step along the way - from blood draw to storage to the moment a sample finally reaches the spectrometer – can leave its own mark on the resulting fingerprint measurement.\nThe new paper from the BIRD team, published in Analytical Chemistry puts that question to the test. Across more than 600 infrared spectroscopic measurements, they benchmarked the variables that matter most in practice: Whether blood draw at the clinic, freezing, thawing, or tube filling actually shows up in an infrared fingerprint, and whether it matters how long a sample waits before it is finally being measured. Each effect was then weighed against something more fundamental – the natural biological variability between people.\nThese findings provide practical guidance for standardizing IMF workflows across clinical studies, laboratories, and biobanks. Our research could make the current healthcare system more effective and improve the quality of preventive medicine, with the possibility of safeguarding our health in the future.\nWhat is preventive medicine?\nMedicine was developed to provide help with illnesses and to treat health problems that compromise a person’s well-being. As it was soon realized, especially with epidemics, preventing the spread of disease was easier than treating a fully developed condition. Thus, preventive medicine was conceptualized to forego disease occurrence and halt the progression of clinical conditions by applying measures in advance.\nControlling communicable diseases has been especially effective, and during the 20th century, these efforts radically decreased the number of premature deaths. Over recent decades, however, significant changes have taken place, as from the mid-1990s, the burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) has vastly surpassed the impact of infections. NCDs, which comprise two-thirds of the global disease burden, are responsible for 70% of mortalities worldwide, while in Hungary, 94% of all deaths are caused by NCDs.\nFour main NCDs account for the vast majority of premature deaths: cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes, and chronic respiratory disease. So these four are the major targets of preventive care. Prevention strategies aim to stop disease development at an incipient stage as early as the risk becomes evident. So risk factors (conditions predisposing to disease) are identified before they cause any symptoms. Clinical screening for risk factors occurs in healthy individuals in the context of primary care. Among the NCDs, cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the most prevalent, and it is widely believed to be largely preventable: 80% of CVD deaths might be avoided by early detection and proper management of risk factors. The interventions include a combination of lifestyle changes (dietary changes, promotion of physical activity and weight loss) and pharmacological therapy. The application of appropriate treatment, which helps prevent the development of clinical disease, is known as primary prevention, as it focuses on preventing diseases from occurring.\nPrimary prevention is less effective in Hungary than in Western European countries, and this issue is the main cause of the shorter healthy lifespan in the country.\nWhat is personalized medicine?\nWhile a disease is believed to indicate a homogenous entity caused by a unique underlying process, it may cause a wide range of symptoms that also vary in severity and pattern in each individual. Similarly, disease development is not a unified process: in a group of people who apparently share the same characteristics of predisposition, some present earlier with clinical disease than others. Furthermore, disease progression also shows a high degree of variability in people. In this case, as it seems obvious, the one size fits all approach will not suffice, as it cannot provide equal benefit to all people. Instead, a strategy is needed to reduce the risk of disease with the use of differentiated care in individuals. This is achieved by tailor-made prevention steps and individualized therapy, using stratification to set up subgroups of people with similar risk levels and by applying a treatment plan based on the risk category. An even more sophisticated approach is foreseen in the future, with further individualization, providing personal care based on a more detailed risk assessment. We anticipate that laser-based, population-wide screening will contribute to preventing many premature deaths in increasing life expectancy.\nShow allShow less\nOctober 29, 2024\nLaser science in healthcare and in medicine\nWhen Theodore H. Maiman unveiled the first functional laser on July 7, 1960, in New York, it was hard to conceive of the range of applications that such high-intensity beams of tightly collimated light would one day find. But within a year, it made its debut as a surgical instrument in ophthalmology when it was tested on a patient in the US. And laser physicists have yet to run out of ideas and applications.\nMedicine profits enormously from lasers. Lasers are used as high-precision scalpels. Unlike finely machined knives, the beam does not come into direct contact with the underlying tissue, making the device inherently sterile. A laser beam heats the skin and cuts it open or, if necessary, destroys it with pinpoint accuracy. There is no bleeding during treatment because the heat of the radiation immediately cauterizes the veins.\nThis also makes lasers suitable for stopping bleeding in a targeted way, even in places that are difficult to access. The laser beam reaches the affected area directly via endoscopes or light conductors and can thus stop internal bleeding in the stomach, for example. Laser light can also reach blood vessels directly via optical fibers and clear veins of unwanted deposits and blockages (arteriosclerosis) that could potentially lead to a heart attack.\nLikewise, lasers can be used to remove superficial skin deformities such as port-wine stains or to erase tattoos by evaporating the pigments in the skin. They are also playing an increasing role in the diagnosis and treatment of tumors. Smaller tumors in the body that can be reached directly, such as skin cancer, can now be removed using lasers by killing the cancerous cells. Laser-guided computer tomography helps to obtain cross-sectional images of the body. The method is less dangerous and less costly than X-ray and nuclear spin procedures, which, however, still have a higher resolution than imaging methods.\nPulsed lasers in the infrared radiation range have found an application in dentistry. Since the laser radiation heats up embedded water and as there is more water in a decayed tooth than in a healthy tooth, a tooth damaged in this way can be treated effectively without destroying the neighboring healthy teeth. In addition, it is possible to precisely scan the shape of a tooth using laser radiation. With the help of the data, a dental prosthesis can be produced optimally and precisely.\nIn ophthalmology, laser surgery is used to treat myopia, short-sightedness, and long-sightedness. Both conditions can be corrected by altering the curvature of the cornea, either by laser ablation of corneal substance (myopia) or by raising the level of the cornea (long-sightedness). As the uppermost corneal layer is not damaged, scar formation is avoided.\nAs we can see, lasers are already an indispensable part of medical technology. This new laser technology is more sensitive than current methods, with a finer nose for disorders.\nShow allShow less\nOctober 21, 2024\nThe finest fractions of time\nThe quantum world challenges our everyday intuitions, including our notions of time. Electronic transitions in atoms take place within attoseconds. An attosecond is a billionth of a billionth of a second (10-18 sec). Prof. Dr. Ferenc Krausz and the scientists in the attoworld research group in Garching, run jointly by the Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics (MPQ) and Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (LMU), study electron motions using ultrashort light pulses of this order.\nIn the world of electrons, things happen very, very fast. The faster objects move, the harder it becomes to observe them. A human heartbeat lasts for about a second – a timespan readily visible to the eye. To capture changes that take less than 0.2 sec, we have to use technologies that slow time down – by freezing the motions at shorter intervals – as in time-lapse photography.\nThis principle allows us to follow the millisecond wingbeats of flies. In order to perceive the trajectory of a bullet shot from a gun, time must be slowed by a factor of 200,000. And the active components of electronic circuits take less than a nanosecond to switch on or off.\nMolecules rotate in a matter of picoseconds. To image the vibrations of the chemical bonds between their atoms, one must increase the frame rate by another factor of 1,000 as each oscillation takes femtoseconds, in other words millionths of a billionth of a second (10-15 sec).\nTo study the motions of the electrons in atoms or molecules, the shutter speed must be reduced to a few attoseconds. Attoworld's physicists routinely produce laser pulses in this range. And these ultrashort flashes make it possible to observe the dynamics of elementary particles in real time. For the first time, we have a direct window into a hitherto mysterious realm.\nThe goal is to understand and control the motion of electrons upon interaction with the electric light field of ultrashort pulses. The initial events take place as the electrons are being accelerated by the changing electric field of the incoming pulse on an attosecond time scale. This can then induce chemical follow-up reactions that may be relevant even for understanding biochemical processes in our body. The fast-changing electric field of ultrashort pulses can also be used to accelerate charged particles like electrons or protons. While infrared fingerprints may distinguish lung cancer, they do not yet inform us about the individual blood components that make up the difference. Nevertheless, it would be good to know their identity to be able to further improve the method. This is what we demonstrated in a new study just published in Angewandte Chemie (DOI: 10.1002/anie.202103272). It is all about a combination of two techniques that are usually applied separately: mass spectrometry and infrared spectroscopy. The aim was to decode the actual chemical changes behind the previously “black box” infrared fingerprints of lung cancer. Now, with mass spectrometry of blood samples performed at the Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry in Munich, we identified a set of 12 proteins that account for the spectral signature of lung cancer, where early diagnostic markers are currently missing. All of these proteins were known since a long time. Now - like old dogs playing new tricks - the combinatorial protein signature that we defined turns a new page in diagnostic efforts. And this signature can be measured in a matter of minutes using infrared light!\nSo are we now one step closer to capturing disease and defining health? Certainly so. Especially as laser scientists at our department are engineering new ways of delivering ever shorter and more precise pulses of light for spectroscopic investigations. Metaphorically, this is like a magnifying lens that allows us to inspect the molecular zoo in our blood at once – in a snapshot. Finally, the results are of broader relevance for many disciplines, as one may generalize our findings to detection of other diseases that leave their traces in blood.\nYet, while we are working on new advances in capturing human health by shining light through drops of blood, we are bearing in mind the notion of Isaak Newton: “What we know is a drop, what we don’t know is an ocean.”.\nMihaela Zigman\nOriginal article:\nAngew Chem Int Ed Engl\nMolecular Origin of Blood-based Infrared Spctroscopic Fingerprints\nLiudmila Voronina, Cristina Leonardo, Johannes B Mueller-Reif, Philipp E Geyer, Marinus Huber, Michael Trubetskov, Kosmas V Kepesidis, Jürgen Behr, Matthias Mann, Krausz Ferenc, Mihaela Žigman\nPMID: 33881784\nDOI: 10.1002 / anie.202103272\nhttps://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/anie.202103272\nhttps://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ange.202107126\nShow allShow less\nMay 28, 2021\n“Electrons for life” went live in Vienna\nAfter a very long pause due to the pandemic, the chance to listen to a lecture and talk to Ferenc Krausz in person took place just on May 28th in Vienna. It was a special occasion. Not only in a city significant for attoscience but also special to the Hungarian-Austrian scientist Ferenc Krausz who worked there over many years. The Austrian Academy of Sciences (OeAW) held its Ceremonial Congress of 2021 with renowned scientists lead by Anton Zeilinger, president of the OeAW, as well as Austrian president Alexander Van der Bellen, welcoming Ferenc Krausz as the keynote speaker.\nAnyone that would like to watch the ceremonial presentation, seeing the results of Ferenc Krausz and his team from the CMF, LMU and MPQ, here you get the chance to see the video: https://youtu.be/4dQn4fe33hc\nIn a wake of this impulsive lecture, the main Austrian broadcasting house (ORF) held an interview with Ferenc Krausz. And right here you have the chance to listen and read on the interview with journalist Robert Czepel and learn about what happened in the cellar laboratory of the TU Vienna about two decades ago: https://science.orf.at/stories/3206849/\nShow allShow less\nMarch 13, 2021\nTaking it personally: A new blood-based test for monitoring health\nA new study carried out by a team of laser physicists, molecular biologists and physicians based at LMU Munich and the Max Planck Institute for Quantum Optics has confirmed the temporal stability of the molecular composition of blood in a population of healthy individuals. The data provide a basis for a new method of monitoring the constituents of blood and detecting alterations that reveal changes in a person’s state of health.\nThe molecular composition of the blood provides information regarding one’s state of health, and may be compared to an individual fingerprint. In principle, changes in the constituents of blood can serve as early signs of disease. However, before chemical fingerprints can be utilized for diagnostic purposes, the stability of the molecular patterns in healthy persons over time must be firmly established. Researchers under the direction of Dr. Mihaela Žigman, Head of the Broadband Infrared Diagnostics (BIRD) group in the Department of Laser Physics led by Prof. Ferenc Krausz at LMU Munich, in collaboration with Prof. Dr. Nadia Harbeck at the LMU Medical Centre, have now successfully accomplished this task. With the aid of a method known as Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), the team has shown that the molecular composition of blood samples obtained from a cohort of healthy donors remains stable over a period of several months, and confirmed that each of the resulting spectra could be clearly assigned to an individual person.\nRapid diagnosis of human diseases is a long standing problem in medicine. As diseases often alter the molecular make-up of circulating body fluids, obtaining a snapshot of their molecular composition would be invaluable in detecting a multitude of diseased states, and the types and concentrations of the many molecules found in the bloodstream can provide vital information on a person’s health. The real challenge, however, comes when one tries to determine the exact composition of body fluids, given that the concentrations of informative molecules are often extremely low. The interdisciplinary BIRD team led by Dr. Mihaela Žigman in Prof. Dr. Ferenc Krausz’s department at LMU, in collaboration with Prof. Dr. Nadia Harbeck at the LMU Medical Centre, has now investigated the stability of the chemical make-up of blood samples over days, weeks and even months.\nBased on Fourier-transform infrared measurements (FTIR), the researchers analysed the molecular fingerprints of serum and plasma samples obtained from 31 healthy individuals over the clinically relevant period of 6 months. The study demonstrated that the infrared molecular fingerprint of each individual donor in fact remained stable over periods ranging from a few days to weeks and months, and each temporal profile could be readily attributed to the participant concerned.\n“This newly revealed temporal stability of blood-based infrared fingerprints provides a basis for future applications of minimally invasive infrared spectroscopy as a reliable method for the future of health monitoring,” says Mihaela Žigman, leader of the research group.\nStandard Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, which uses conventional light sources, could soon be replaced by chemical analyses based on infrared lasers. Given the much higher intensity of laser light, the latter method should be more sensitive and precise, and should therefore yield more detailed and informative characterizations of the molecular constituents of blood. The physicists in the attoworld team, led by Prof. Ferenc Krausz, are now working on the laser technologies necessary to achieve this aim. Exposure to intense infrared light causes molecules to vibrate and emit light at specific frequencies, which depend on the chemical structures of the molecules within the sample. Analysis of the components of the resulting spectrum of electromagnetic oscillations enables researchers to assign them to the many types of molecules present in body fluids. As Prof. Krausz and colleagues reported last year, the new method allows minuscule amounts of different classes of molecules to be spectroscopically detected (Nature, 2. January 2020; doi 10.1038/s41586-019-1850-7).\n“With our lasers, we can already detect electrical signals emitted by excited molecules with very high sensitivity,” Ferenc Krausz explains. “Such precise measurements of alterations in the molecular composition of body fluids, together with knowledge of the stable molecular fingerprint of healthy controls, opens up new analytical opportunities in biology and medicine,” says Marinus Huber, leading author of the study. “Our results reveal that it is possible to obtain informative, blood-based infrared fingerprints efficiently, repeatedly and in a minimally invasive manner. The key, in this case, is that the analysis ought to be sensitive enough and sufficiently broad to cover a wide range of possible molecules (or types of molecules) - to be in position to monitor personal health and detect disorders at an early stage. Practically speaking, following-up a person’s health status regularly might become paramount for timely-detecting relevant deviations. In addition to its uses in the fields of health monitoring and preventive medicine, systems biology shall also benefit from the availability of the approach,” Mihaela Žigman adds.\n-Thorsten Naeser\nOriginal Publication:\nHuber, M., Kepesidis, K.V., Voronina, L. et al. Stability of person-specific blood-based infrared molecular fingerprints opens up prospects for health monitoring. Nat Commun 12, 1511 (2021).\nhttps://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-21668-5\nhttps://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-21668-5\nFurther information is available from:\nDr. Mihaela Žigman\nLudwig-Maximilians-University Munich\nAm Coulombwall 1\n85748 Garching, Germany.\nE-Mail: mihaela.zigman@cmf.hu.\nShow allShow less\nLoad more\nMarch 11, 2020\nSample storage at its best\nCMF’s strategic partner, the Ludwig-Maximilians-University (LMU) in Munich, Germany, just installed an automated biobanking system for sample storage at temperatures below minus 150°C. What is this good for? Under these very low temperatures - so called “cryogenic” conditions in the atmosphere above liquid nitrogen - human samples, such as blood plasma or actually any biological tissues, can be kept for several years, decades without sample deterioration.\nIt assures that valuable human materials collected in frame of clinical studies can be used in long term and thus enables researchers to analyze these with molecular fingerprinting techniques most efficiently. Such an automated cryogenic system is made of large tightly sealed tank that is capable to store up to 60,000 samples. The system is further equipped with a robotic arm that can pick individual tubes automatically, such that the samples are kept and handled well below minus 100 °C at all times.\nThis installation has a direct impact for the future of the joint CMF-LMU research aims. On the one hand the two institutions will be conducting joint clinical studies. On the other, LMU biobanking system also serves as a test case for the CMF’s envisioned own biorepository, to be established in Budapest.\nThus, CMF is getting familiar with the best way to store most valuable biological materials for the years of research to come!\nShow allShow less\nJanuary 7, 2020\nField-resolved infrared spectroscopy of biological systems\nIn cooperation between the Laboratory of Attosecond Physics at the Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics and the Centre for Advanced Laser Applications of the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, the King Saud University Riad and the Center for Molecular Fingerprinting (Budapest, Hungary), we have developed a molecular spectroscopy technique that overcomes long-standing limitations of traditional techniques, like Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, as described in our recent publication.\nA powerful femtosecond laser delivers 28 million pulses per second, with highly repeatable waveforms, comprising merely a few infrared-electric-field oscillations. Transmitting these pulses through a complex, molecular sample synchronously excites infrared-active vibrations of molecular bonds, each at its own eigenfrequency. The signals emitted by the vibrationally-excited molecules in the wake of the impulsive excitation coherently add up to a ‘molecular fingerprint’ characteristic of the sample’s molecular composition.\nIn contrast to traditional spectroscopies, where the entire response of the sample to an infrared excitation hits the detector(s), in field-resolved spectroscopy sub-optical-cycle portions of the time-domain fingerprint field are sequentially carved out by means of nonlinear optics. This dramatically reduces any infrared background on the measured signals, including the noise originating from the excitation and thermal background. This conceptional advance results in an unprecedented detection sensitivity and dynamic range.\nWe have also demonstrated first biological applications that have so far been beyond the reach of infrared vibrational spectroscopies. These applications include first high-signal-to-noise ratio infrared transmission measurements of living biological tissue and fingerprinting of liquid biopsies with sub-µg/ml sensitivity. Thus, field-resolved spectroscopy promises improved molecular sensitivity and molecular coverage for probing complex, real-world biological and medical settings.\nShow allShow less\nDecember 16, 2019\nProf. Ferenc Krausz has recieved the honorary membership of the Roland Eötvös Physical Society\nProf. Ferenc Krausz has recieved the honorary membership of the Roland Eötvös Physical Society, Budapest. After receiving the membership the laser physicist of the Ludwig-Maximilians University München and the Max-Planck-Institute of Quantum Optics held an lecture about how attosecond science technologies can in the future contribute to a new way of finding molecules in human biofluids like blood.\nThis may path the way for medical applications to detect diseases by analyzing so called molecular fingerprints with the help of strong laser light pulses.\nShow allShow less\nContact\nContact\nIf you are interested in our study and would like to get further information, please get in touch with This:\nPhysicist Barry C. Barish, who won the 2017 Nobel Prize in physics for the discovery of gravitational waves, will join the faculty of the University of California, Riverside, on Sept. 1.\nBarish, the Linde Professor of Physics, Emeritus, at Caltech, shared the Nobel Prize with fellow Caltech physicist Kip Thorne and MIT physicist Rainer Weiss. The prize recognized their “decisive contributions to the LIGO detector and the observation of gravitational waves.”\nOn Sept. 14, 2015, LIGO, or the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, detected for the first time gravitational waves predicted by Albert Einstein more than 100 years ago. A collision between two black holes generated the waves, which took 1.3 billion years to arrive at the LIGO detector. Barish brought the LIGO project to completion, enabling the first observation of this phenomenon.\n“We are delighted that Professor Barish is joining our faculty,” said Cynthia Larive, UCR provost and executive vice chancellor. “He will be a strong inspiration for our students, researchers, and faculty. His hiring reflects the growing prominence of our research and graduate programs and the enormous effort UCR invests in our students to prepare them for research at the highest levels. We are grateful UCR will benefit from Professor Barish’s extraordinary achievements.”\nBarish earned his bachelor’s degree in physics in 1957 and his doctorate in experimental particle physics in 1962 from UC Berkeley. He joined Caltech as a postdoc in 1963, became a professor in 1966, and was appointed Linde Professor of Physics in 1991. He led the LIGO effort from its inception through the final design stages, and in subsequent discoveries. In 1997, he created the LIGO Scientific Collaboration, which enables more than 1000 collaborators worldwide to participate in LIGO.\nHe has served on many important science committees, including co-chairing the subpanel of the High Energy Physics Advisory Panel that developed a long-range plan for U.S. high-energy physics in 2001. He chaired the Commission of Particles and Fields and the U.S. Liaison Committee to the International Union of Pure and Applied Physics, and has also been active in a variety of international physics collaborations.\n“I very much look forward to joining the UCR physics faculty with its exciting research programs and orientation toward student success,” Barish said. “I hope to bring some new research perspectives, and especially, to helping educate the very special UCR student body.”\nBarish is the recipient of the Fudan-Zhongzhi Science Award (China), Princess of Asturias Prize for Science and Technology (Spain), Giuseppe and Vanna Cocconi Prize from the European Physical Society, the Enrico Fermi Prize from the Italian Physical Society, and the Klopsteg Award from the American Association of Physics Teachers. He is a member of the National Academy of Sciences, which awarded him the Henry Draper Medal. From 2003 to 2010, he served as a presidential appointee to the National Science Board.\nBarish is an elected member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and a fellow of both the American Association for the Advancement of Science and of the American Physical Society, where he also served as president. He has received honorary doctorates from the University of Bologna, the University of Florida, and the University of Glasgow.\nWorking with UCR students — especially as a first-generation college student himself — was a major factor is Barish’s decision to join the faculty in the Department of Physics and Astronomy in the College of Natural and Agricultural Sciences.\nKathryn Uhrich, the dean of the college, noted Barish’s work has “tremendously impacted the field of astrophysics.”\n“We are truly grateful for Professor Barish’s willingness to share his wealth of groundbreaking research and knowledge with UCR students and faculty, who also work every day to follow his example and push the boundaries of science,” she said. “That we have two Nobel Prize winners joining our faculty puts us in rare company among international universities and speaks to the quality of our institution — its people, research, learning, and progress.”\nBarish is the second Nobel laureate to join UCR. Last month, Richard Schrock, a Nobel Prize-winning chemist and UC Riverside alumnus, announced he was joining the faculty.\nRecently, Barish and Schrock were inducted as honorary academicians into the Royal Academy of European Doctors, based in Spain.\nShare this Article\nMedia Contacts\nTags\nscience/technology\nBarry Barish\nCollege Of Natural And Agricultural Sciences\nDepartment Of Physics And Astronomy\nNobel Laureate\nNobel Prize\nPress Release\nScience / Technology\nRelated Articles\nUCR campus as seen from a drone\nSocial Science / Education\nUCR receives $8 million in federal grants\nAI image of geothermal facility\nScience / Technology\nDepartment of Energy awards AI geothermal project to UCs\nDepressed woman\nHealth\nMental health stigma in Japan may deter care\nQuantum electrons\nScience / Technology\nUCR physicist selected as an Experimental Physics Investigator by Moore Foundation\nSearch\nUniversity of California, Riverside\n900 University Ave.\nRiverside, CA 92521\nTel: (951) 827-1012\nUCR Library\nCampus Status\nCampus Store\nCareer Opportunities\nEspañol\nMaps and Directions\nVisit UCR\nUniversity of California, Riverside\n900 University Ave.\nRiverside, CA 92521\ntel: (951) 827-1012\nemail: webmaster@ucr.edu\nFind Us\nView campus map\nFollow Us:\nUC Riverside Facebook\nUC Riverside X\nUC Riverside YouTube\nUC Riverside Instagram\nUC Riverside on LinkedIn\nUC Riverside TikTok\nUC Riverside on Threads\nRelated Links\nCan I Bug You? articles\n2021\nMay 2021\n“The timing is perfect”\n“The timing is perfect”\nRenowned planetary researcher and Nobel laureate Didier Queloz is moving to ETH Zurich, where he will be joining with other professors to study the origins of life in a new centre.\n21.05.2021\nby\nFelix Würsten\nRead\nNumber of comments\nDidier Queloz\nDidier Queloz will head a new centre at ETH Zurich that will address a fundamental scientific question. (Image: University of Geneva)\nIn 1995, together with his doctoral advisor Michel Mayor, Didier Queloz caused an international furore. At the University of Geneva, the two Swiss astronomers discovered the first exoplanet orbiting a solar-type star. The duo garnered the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics for their groundbreaking discovery.\nIn recent years, Queloz, who not only holds a chair at the University of Geneva but has also been a professor at the University of Cambridge’s Cavendish Laboratory since 2013, has participated in the detection of numerous other planets. At the same time, the focus of his research is increasingly on searching for planets that are potentially habitable, hoping thereby to find greater insight into how life on Earth may have originated.\nThis summer, Didier Queloz is leaving his alma mater to take up his post as Professor of Physics at ETH Zurich where, as designated director, he will help establish the new ETH Center for the Origin and Prevalence of Life with the involvement of professors from five departments.\nMr. Queloz, what made you decide to accept a professorship in Zurich?\nDidier Queloz: The reason for my move is very simple: ETH Zurich is working on an absolutely fantastic project. We intend to explore a new area of research that focuses on the origin of life. The timing is perfect.\nWhy’s that?\nIn recent years, rapid progress relevant to this topic has been made in various research fields. In my own area, astronomy, we have discovered thousands of new planets, including smaller stellar objects, that could support life. We were able to detect atmospheres on a number of planets and now know a fair bit about the composition of these celestial bodies. The second key field is researching our own planetary system, particularly the exploration of Mars. Mars is enormously important for our work because its development over the first billion years was very similar to that of Earth. Not much has happened on Mars since then, while plate tectonics have caused dramatic changes in the surface of Earth. Mars shows us what Earth may have looked like some 3.5 billion years ago.\nWhy is that crucial in unravelling the origin of life?\nIt’s important because that is when it is assumed that life began on Earth – perhaps on Mars, too. Moreover, other objects in our solar system also warrant a closer look: Venus, for instance, or Jupiter’s moons. These objects reveal the potential composition of the different exoplanets.\nBut don’t we also need biologists and chemists if we want to investigate the origin of life?\nYes, their expertise is also vital. In the last few years, considerable strides have been made in biochemistry and molecular chemistry as well. Today, biochemists can use computers to calculate completely new compounds and are able to simulate networks of chemical reactions. These networks probably served as catalysts for the origins of life. Geoscientists, too, are indispensable as they can tell us what conditions were like on Earth when life evolved.\nAnd the new centre will bring all these different fields together?\nYes. Advances in the aforementioned fields have completely changed the status quo. It is imperative that these disciplines now join forces in order for us to take the next step. My experience in Cambridge shows that interdisciplinary dialogue helps bring forth new ideas. A new community is currently forming at large universities such as Harvard and Caltech, as well as Cambridge. Researchers from very different fields aim to work together in solving a fundamental problem. It’s still unclear how far we’ll get but we predict that we will be able to make great progress over the next few years.\n“\"It is imperative that the different disciplines now join forces in order for us to take the next step.\" ”\nDidier Queloz\nSo this community hasn’t been established at ETH Zurich yet?\nThere are plenty of fantastic researchers at ETH Zurich and quite a few who plan to head in precisely this direction. ETH Zurich has the potential to lead the field in this regard, which will also boost Switzerland’s standing as a hotspot for research.\nWhat will it take for this new community to get off the ground?\nYou have to be prepared to venture into the uncharted territory between the established disciplines. That’s challenging, but also rewarding. I used to have the naïve notion that I would be able to prove that extraterrestrial life exists if I could find oxygen in a planet’s atmosphere. Geochemists showed me that this idea is too simplistic. I didn’t hear this from other astronomers but from scientists in a very different subject area. Interdisciplinary dialogue helps you question your own conclusions and realise if they are incorrect.\nAnd what is needed at the institutional level?\nGood networking is essential, both within ETH Zurich and in the international arena. To attract talented young academics, we have to raise awareness that we are researching a fundamental issue at ETH Zurich. But that’s not enough: we also have to offer the next generation of researchers good prospects so they can establish themselves in this field.\nWhat do you see as your specific role at ETH Zurich?\nFirst of all, I can contribute my astrophysical expertise. With my team, I will continue to look for new planets that could support life. That will still be my core topic. Furthermore, I can bring my experience to bear in terms of how to set up networks and address research issues that don’t fit neatly into any one traditional field. ETH Zurich boasts a great deal of creativity, which we now have to develop to the full. In this sense, I see my role as a builder of bridges.\n“\"Is there life on these planets? Everyone is obsessed with this question. We should turn this potential to our advantage.\"”\nDidier Queloz\nYou seem to be fascinated by the topic. Do you also consider yourself an ambassador?\nIt’s actually quite remarkable. Nowadays, we have an excellent understanding of the composition of living organisms, of how our bodies function and how to cure diseases. But how did it all start? How exactly did life come into being? We still don’t know. It’s a fundamental question, similar to the origin of the universe or the beginning of time. And who knows: maybe by examining this all-important question, we will discover completely new applications in the field of medicine. To give you one prime example: we all use GPS navigation systems every day as a matter of course. But if Albert Einstein hadn’t formulated his theory of relativity more than 100 years ago, this technology wouldn’t exist today. Schutz\nSherry Suyu[3]\nSaul Teukolsky\nMichele Vallisneri\nClifford Martin Will\nKip Stephen Thorne (born June 1, 1940) is an American astrophysicist and author. He shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics with Rainer Weiss and Barry C. Barish \"for decisive contributions to the LIGO detector and the observation of gravitational waves\".[4][5][6][7][8]\nWith John A. Wheeler and Charles Misner, he coauthored the general relativity textbook Gravitation in 1973. He has also written popular science, notably Black Holes and Time Warps in 1994 which was awarded the Phi Beta Kappa Award in Science for that year.[9]\nThorne was the Richard P. Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics at Caltech from 1991 until 2009.[10] A longtime friend and colleague of Stephen Hawking and Carl Sagan, he advised Sagan on the physics of wormholes for his novel Contact. He was a scientific consultant for Christopher Nolan's films Interstellar[11][12] and Tenet.[13] He received the 2018 Lewis Thomas Prize for science writing.[14]\nLife and career\n[edit]\nDiscussion in the main lecture hall at the École de Physique des Houches (Les Houches Physics School), 1972. From left, Yuval Ne'eman, Bryce DeWitt, Thorne, Demetrios Christodoulou.\nThorne was born on June 1, 1940, in Logan, Utah. His father, D. Wynne Thorne (1908–1979), was a professor of soil chemistry at Utah State University, and his mother, Alison (née Comish; 1914–2004), was an economist and the first woman to receive a PhD in economics from Iowa State College.[15][16] Raised in an academic environment, two of his four siblings also became professors.[17][18] Thorne's parents were members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church) and raised Thorne in the LDS faith, though he now identifies as an atheist. Shortly before his mother's death, she urged Kip and his siblings to leave the LDS Church because of its discrimination against women, which they all did. Regarding his views on science and religion, Thorne has stated: \"There are large numbers of my finest colleagues who are quite devout and believe in God .... There is no fundamental incompatibility between science and religion. I happen to not believe in God.\"[19][20]\nThorne excelled at academics early in life, winning recognition in the Westinghouse Science Talent Search as a senior at Logan High School.[21] He received his BS in physics degree from Caltech in 1962, and his master and PhD in physics from Princeton University in 1964 and 1965 under the supervision of John Archibald Wheeler with a doctoral dissertation on Geometrodynamics of Cylindrical Systems.[22]\nHe returned to Caltech as an associate professor in 1967 and became a professor of theoretical physics in 1970, becoming one of the youngest full professors in the history of Caltech at age 30. He became the William R. Kenan Jr. Professor in 1981, and the Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics in 1991. He was an adjunct professor at the University of Utah from 1971 to 1998 and Andrew D. White Professor at Large at Cornell University from 1986 to 1992.[23] Since 2009, Thorne has been the Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics, emeritus.[24]\nThorne and Linda Jean Peterson married in 1960. Their children are Kares Anne and Bret Carter, an architect. Thorne and Peterson divorced in 1977. Thorne was set up on a blind date with Lynda Obst, later a film producer, by physicist Carl Sagan. They dated in 1979–1980, and parted and remained friends, to the extent that they later collaborated on the movie Interstellar.[25] Thorne and his second wife, Carolee Joyce Winstein, a professor of biokinesiology and physical therapy at USC, married in 1984.[26] In 2015, he collaborated with Obst and Stephen Hawking on a movie script, for which they wrote several drafts.[27][28]\nThroughout the years, Thorne has served as a mentor and thesis advisor to many students who became leaders in observational, experimental, or astrophysical aspects of general relativity. Approximately 50 physicists have received PhDs at Caltech under Thorne's personal mentorship.[10]\nThorne is known for his ability to convey the excitement and significance of discoveries in gravitation and astrophysics to both professional and lay audiences. His presentations on subjects such as black holes, gravitational radiation, relativity, time travel, and wormholes have been included in PBS shows in the U.S. and on the BBC in the United Kingdom.[citation needed]\nIn 2017, Thorne gave the George Gamow Memorial Lecture at the University of Colorado Boulder, on “Probing the Warped Side of the Universe with Gravitational Waves: From the Big Bang to Black Holes.”[29]\nResearch\n[edit]\nThorne in 1972\nThorne's research has principally focused on relativistic astrophysics and gravitation physics, with emphasis on relativistic stars, black holes and especially gravitational waves.[10] He is perhaps best known to the public for his controversial theory that wormholes can conceivably be used for time travel.[30] However, Thorne's scientific contributions, which center on the general nature of space, time, and gravity, span the full range of topics in general relativity.\nGravitational waves and LIGO\n[edit]\nThorne's work has dealt with the prediction of gravitational wave strengths and their temporal signatures as observed on Earth. These \"signatures\" are of great relevance to LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory), a multi-institution gravitational wave experiment for which Thorne has been a leading proponent – in 1984, he cofounded the LIGO Project (the largest project ever funded by the NSF[31]) to discern and measure any fluctuations between two or more 'static' points; such fluctuations would be evidence of gravitational waves, as calculations describe. A significant aspect of his research is developing the mathematics necessary to analyze these objects.[32] Thorne also carries out engineering design analyses for features of the LIGO that cannot be developed on the basis of experiment and he gives advice on data analysis algorithms by which the waves will be sought. He has provided theoretical support for LIGO, including identifying gravitational wave sources that LIGO should target, designing the baffles to control scattered light in the LIGO beam tubes, and – in collaboration with Vladimir Braginsky's (Moscow, Russia) research group – inventing quantum nondemolition designs for advanced gravity-wave detectors and ways to reduce the most serious kind of noise in advanced detectors: thermoelastic noise. With Carlton M. Caves, Thorne invented the back-action-evasion approach to quantum nondemolition measurements of the harmonic oscillators – a technique applicable both in gravitational wave detection and quantum optics.[10]\nOn February 11, 2016, a team of four physicists[a] representing the LIGO Scientific Collaboration, announced that in September 2015, LIGO recorded the signature of two black holes colliding 1.3 billion light-years away. This recorded detection was the first direct observation of the fleeting chirp of a gravitational wave and confirmed a prediction of the general theory of relativity.[33][34][35][36][37]\nBlack hole cosmology\n[edit]\nMain article: Hoop conjecture\nA cylindrical bundle of magnetic field lines\nIn 1963–1964, Thorne's PhD mentor at Princeton, John Wheeler, assigned him a problem to think about: find out whether or not a cylindrical bundle of repulsive magnetic field lines will implode under its own attractive gravitational force. After several months wrestling with the problem, he proved that it was impossible for cylindrical magnetic field lines to implode.[38]: 262–265\nThorne determined that the gravitational force can overcome all interior pressure only when an object has been compressed in all directions, as in the case of a spherical star imploding under gravitational force. To express this realization, he proposed his hoop conjecture, which describes an imploding star turning into a black hole when the critical circumference of the designed hoop can be placed around it and set into rotation. That is, any object of mass M around which a hoop of circumference can be spun must be a black hole.[38]: 266–267 [39]: 189–190\nThorne and his students have developed an approach to the theory of black holes called the \"membrane paradigm\", and used it to clarify the Blandford–Znajek mechanism by which black holes may power some quasars and active galactic nuclei.[38]: 405–411\nThorne has investigated the quantum statistical mechanical origin of the entropy of a black hole. With his postdoc Wojciech Zurek, he showed that the entropy of a black hole is the logarithm of the number of ways that the hole could have been made.[38]: 445–446\nWith Igor Novikov and Don Page, he developed the general relativistic theory of thin accretion disks around black holes, and using this theory he deduced that with a doubling of its mass by such accretion a black hole will be spun up to 0.998 of the maximum spin allowed by general relativity, but not any farther. This is probably the maximum black-hole spin allowed in nature.[10]\nWormholes and time travel\n[edit]\nA wormhole is a short cut connecting two separate regions in space. In the figure the green line shows the short way through wormhole, and the red line shows the long way through normal space.\nThorne and his co-workers at Caltech conducted scientific research on whether the laws of physics permit space and time to be multiply connected (can there exist classical, traversable wormholes and \"time machines\"?).[40] With Sung-Won Kim, Thorne identified a universal physical mechanism (the explosive growth of vacuum polarization of quantum fields), that may always prevent spacetime from developing closed timelike curves (i.e., prevent backward time travel).[41]\nWith Mike Morris and Ulvi Yurtsever, he showed that traversable wormholes can exist in the structure of spacetime only if they are threaded by quantum fields in quantum states that violate the averaged null energy condition (i.e. have negative renormalized energy spread over a sufficiently large region).[42] This has triggered research to explore the ability of quantum fields to possess such extended negative energy. Recent calculations by Thorne indicate that simple masses passing through traversable wormholes could never engender paradoxes – there are no initial conditions that lead to paradox once time travel is introduced. If his results can be generalized, they would suggest that none of the supposed paradoxes formulated in time travel stories can actually be formulated at a precise physical level: that is, that any situation in a time travel story turns out to permit many consistent solutions.[citation needed]\nRelativistic stars, multipole moments and other endeavors\n[edit]\nWith Anna Żytkow, Thorne predicted the existence of red supergiant stars with neutron-star cores (Thorne–Żytkow objects).[43] He laid the foundations for the theory of pulsations of relativistic stars and the gravitational radiation they emit. With James Hartle, Thorne derived from general relativity the laws of motion and precession of black holes and other relativistic bodies, including the influence of the coupling of their multipole moments to the spacetime curvature of nearby objects,[44] as well as writing down the Hartle-Thorne metric, an approximate solution which describes the exterior of a slowly and rigidly rotating, stationary and axially symmetric body.\nThorne has also theoretically predicted the existence of universally antigravitating \"exotic matter\" – the element needed to accelerate the expansion rate of the universe, keep traversable wormhole \"Star Gates\" open and keep timelike geodesic free float \"warp drives\" working. With Clifford Will[45] and others of his students, he laid the foundations for the theoretical interpretation of experimental tests of relativistic theories of gravity – foundations on which Will and others then built. As of 2005, Thorne was interested in the origin of classical space and time from the quantum foam of quantum gravity theory.[citation needed]\nPublications\n[edit]\nKip Thorne lecture at science festival in Lviv, Ukraine 31.05.25\nKip Thorne lecture in Lviv, Ukraine, May 2025\nIn 1973, Thorne co-authored Gravitation with Charles Misner and John A. Wheeler;[46] that according to John C. Baez and Chris Hillman, is one of the great scientific books of all time and has inspired two generations of students.[47] In 1994, he published Black Holes and Time Warps, a popular science book that traces black holes from John Michell to Stephen Hawking and beyond. It has been published in at least twelve languages: English, German (1994), Spanish (1995), French and Japanese (1997), Greek (1999), Czech (2004), Polish, Chinese and Korean (2005), Thai (2008), and Italian (2013).[48] In 2014, he published The Science of Interstellar, in which he explains the science behind Christopher Nolan's film; Nolan wrote the foreword. In the book Thorne discusses the major role of the fictional black hole Gargantua: \"First a weird claim: Black holes are made from warped space and warped time. Nothing else--no matter whatsoever.\"[49]\nIn September 2017, Thorne and Roger D. Blandford published Modern Classical Physics: Optics, Fluids, Plasmas, Elasticity, Relativity, and Statistical Physics, a graduate-level textbook covering the six major areas of physics listed in the title.[50] With artist Lia Halloran, Thorne used poetry and illustrations to explore astrophysics in The Warped Side of Our Universe.[51]\nThorne has published more than 150 articles in scholarly journals.[52] His articles have appeared in publications such as Scientific American,[53] the McGraw-Hill Yearbook of Science and Technology,[54] and Collier's Encyclopedia,[55] among others.\nHonors
